nameStory: Despite its name, the Ring-necked Duck's 'ring' isn't around its neck at all! The brownish collar around the male's neck is so faint it's nearly impossible to see in the field. The name comes from early specimen collectors who could examine the subtle neck ring up close, but birdwatchers today know this duck better by the obvious white ring around its bill.
description: The Ring-necked Duck is a medium-sized diving duck that's perfectly at home on New England's ponds and lakes. Males sport a striking black head with a purple sheen, black back, and bright white sides that make them look like they're wearing a tuxedo. Females are more subdued in rich browns with a lighter face and distinctive white eye-ring. These compact ducks are smaller than a Mallard, with a rounded head and a bill that shows off a telltale white band.

idTips.label: White Bill Ring
idTips.description: Both males and females show a distinct white band around their dark bill, like a tiny life preserver - this is your best field mark and visible even at a distance

idTips.label: Male's Tuxedo Pattern
idTips.description: Breeding males display bold black and white contrasts - glossy black head and back with bright white sides that flash like a beacon when they turn

idTips.label: Female's White Eye-Ring
idTips.description: Female birds show a prominent white ring around their dark eyes, giving them a distinctive wide-eyed expression against their warm brown plumage

idTips.label: Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch them disappear completely underwater with a quick forward dive, staying submerged for 10-25 seconds before popping back up like a cork

idTips.label: Compact Shape
idTips.description: These ducks have a rounded, almost chunky silhouette with a peaked head that looks triangular in profile, quite different from the sleek lines of other diving ducks

habitat: Ring-necked Ducks prefer smaller, quieter waters than many diving ducks - look for them on wooded ponds, beaver impoundments, and shallow lakes with plenty of aquatic vegetation. They especially love waters with emergent cattails and sedges around the edges, and are often found in the same spots where you might see Wood Ducks. During migration, they may gather on larger lakes but typically stick to sheltered coves and bays.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from mid-March through April, when males are in their sharpest breeding plumage with glossy black heads and crisp white sides. Listen for their soft trilling calls during courtship displays.
seasonality.summer: Most birds move north to breed, but non-breeding individuals may linger on larger lakes. Look for molting birds in late summer when males temporarily lose their bright plumage.
seasonality.fall: Migration brings good numbers from September through November, with mixed flocks of males, females, and young birds. Males begin showing their breeding colors again by late fall.
seasonality.winter: Hardy individuals may overwinter on ice-free waters, particularly larger lakes and coastal ponds. Winter birds often form small flocks and are less wary than during migration.

funFact: Ring-necked Ducks are basically the vegetarians of the diving duck world - while their relatives feast on fish and clams, these ducks dive down to munch on underwater plants, seeds, and the occasional snail, making them much more like aquatic lawn mowers than underwater hunters!
confusionNotes: Ring-necked Ducks are often confused with Lesser and Greater Scaup, but remember 'Ring = Ring' - the white ring around the bill is your giveaway, since scaup have plain grayish bills. Female Ring-necked Ducks also have that distinctive white eye-ring that scaup females lack.
contextualKnowledge: The Ring-necked Duck is a perfect example of why common names can be misleading - the 'ring' you should look for isn't on the neck at all! Early naturalists named specimens based on subtle features visible only in the hand, but modern birdwatchers rely on field marks visible from a distance.
compareHints: Among its Aythya relatives, Ring-necked Duck is the small, vegetarian cousin with the white bill ring. Scaup species are grayer overall with plain bills, Redheads have rusty-colored heads and blue bills, and Canvasbacks are much larger with sloped profiles and long, dark bills. Ring-necked Ducks also prefer smaller, more vegetated waters than most of their diving duck cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Ring-necked Ducks, Greater Scaup lack the white ring around the bill and have much more white on their sides and back.
Among New England's diving ducks in the same genus, Lesser Scaup are most similar to Greater Scaup but have rounder heads and shorter wing stripes.

Among its Aythya relatives in New England, the Redhead's rounded head shape sets it apart from the wedge-headed Canvasback, while its copper (not dark) head distinguishes it from Ring-necked Ducks and scaups.
Among its diving duck relatives, canvasbacks are much larger than ring-necked ducks and scaup, with that unique sloping head profile no other Aythya duck shares.
Among its Aythya relatives, Tufted Duck is most similar to Ring-necked Duck but has the distinctive drooping head tuft and golden (not yellow) eyes.
Among its Aythya relatives in New England, male Common Pochards most resemble Redheads but have deeper red heads and darker eyes.
